David Leyonhjelm The Family Tax Benefit (Tighter Income Test) Bill 2014 cuts government spending by more than $270 million a year by means-testing family tax benefit part A more rigorously. Both the coalition and Labor recognise that welfare payments should be means tested. This may seem an uncontroversial idea, but we should remember that some countries have welfare payments that are not means-tested, like universal age pensions, and we should remember that Labor have a troubled relationship with means-testing. They are proud of their changes in recent years to more rigorously means-test family payments and the private health insurance rebate, but they do not want to means-test access to Medicare, and they defend concessional loans for high-income beneficiaries of higher education. The coalition too have a troubled relationship with means-testing. They have loosened means-testing for the age pension and want the private health insurance rebate to be universal. And both sides have continued tied funding to the states that bans state owned hospitals and schools from imposing fees, even on high-income users of these services. Thanks to this inconsistency on means-testing, I have no great hope of support from either the coalition or Labor. But let me go through the process of making the case for the bill. Family tax benefit part A is a welfare payment. Do not be fooled by the mention of tax in the name. It goes to families regardless of whether or not they pay tax. Current and previous governments have decided that families with the least income need this welfare payment of up to $6,723 per child but that a family's need for it reduces when family income exceeds around $50,000. For each dollar earned over that amount, the welfare payment is reduced by 20c. This arrangement is unremarkable and is unaffected by my bill. Moved to suspend standing orders so debate, amendments and votes on the Omnibus Repeal Day (Spring 2014) Bill 2014, the Amending Acts 1970 to 1979 Repeal Bill 2014 and the Statute Law Revision Bill (No. 2) 2014 could be managed together, saying deregulation and cutting red tape were a priority for the government.

Criticised the day's repeal bills for delivering only $1.8 million in savings while $5.1 million in new compliance costs had been added for motorists the same week, and cited the abolition of the Fishing Industry Policy Council, established in 1991 but which had never met, as an example of the bill's low-value measures.

Opposed Labor's amendment and supported the Omnibus Repeal Day (Spring 2014) Bill 2014, drew on 23 years working in his family business to argue red tape burdens business owners, and praised the Prime Minister and the member for Kooyong for leading the government's deregulation agenda.

Supported the Omnibus Repeal Day (Spring 2014) Bill 2014, said the government had delivered $2.1 billion in reduced compliance costs across 400 measures, cited the previous government's addition of 21,000 new regulations over six years, and noted multifactor productivity had declined by three per cent between 2007 and 2012.

Criticised the three repeal bills for delivering only $1.855 million in total savings, the largest single item being $1.16 million from aged care notification changes, contrasted this with Labor's Seamless National Economy reforms estimated to save $4 billion a year, and raised concerns that changes to the Stronger Futures in the Northern Territory Act would remove a requirement for independent review of alcohol management laws.

Mocked the government's repeal day, said the three bills deliver only $1,855,000 in savings, just 0.1 per cent of the government's claimed $2 billion target, noted Labor had repealed 16,794 acts and regulations while in office without fanfare, and criticised the government for leaving the Independent National Security Legislation Monitor position vacant since April.

Criticised the government for adding $5.1 million in new petrol tax compliance costs on small business service stations while claiming to cut red tape, and questioned whether removing consultation requirements from the Broadcasting Services Act and other communications laws would make legislation harder to interpret in practice.

Argued that the government's second red tape repeal day, removing almost 1,000 pieces of regulation and more than 7,200 pages of legislation, builds on a first repeal day that delivered over $700 million in compliance savings, for a combined net deregulatory saving of more than $2.1 billion.

Argued that the government's deregulation agenda has achieved more than $2 billion in compliance savings, exceeding its original $1 billion target, citing an estimated $76 million saving for 447,000 small businesses freed from GST reporting requirements and $160 million a year for 1.4 million Australians through the MyTax pre-filling service.

Argued that the Omnibus Repeal Day bill and related statute law revision bills are being used to sneak through the resumption of fuel excise indexation without proper debate, noting the increase and the start of prepolling for the Victorian state election will both occur in 12 days.

Argued in support of the Omnibus Repeal Day (Spring 2014) Bill, saying it would repeal nearly 1000 pieces of legislation and cut over $2.1 billion in compliance costs a year, including $88 million in savings from the myGov service and $160 million from the new myTax online tax return system.

Argued in support of the Omnibus Repeal Day (Spring 2014) Bill, saying it would abolish 1000 acts and regulations to deliver $1.2 billion in compliance savings, including $426 million from a one-stop shop for environmental approvals, and criticised the previous government for introducing 21000 new regulations between 2010 and 2013.

Argued in support of the Omnibus Repeal Day (Spring 2014) Bill, saying it would cut over $2.1 billion in red and green tape, and cited a Deloitte Access Economics report estimating red tape compliance work now costs the economy more than $250 billion a year, with more than one in 11 Australians employed in compliance roles.

Argued in support of the Omnibus Repeal Day (Spring 2014) Bill, saying it would benefit more than 13500 small businesses in the electorate of Durack by cutting red tape in areas such as communications, environment and aged care, and cited a Productivity Commission finding that small businesses spend up to 5 hours a week on compliance.
Argued in support of the Omnibus Repeal Day (Spring 2014) Bill, praising colleagues' contributions identifying small regulatory burdens he described, echoing another member, as barnacles on the hull.

Argued in support of the Omnibus Repeal Day (Spring 2014) Bill, saying Australia ranked 124th out of 148 nations for burden of government regulation according to the World Economic Forum, and criticised the previous government for introducing 21000 new regulations while the mining tax cost the tax office $50 million to establish.

Argued in support of the Omnibus Repeal Day (Spring 2014) Bill, saying it brings total red tape savings to $2.1 billion, and noted the bill would abolish the Fishing Industry Policy Council, which has never met since being established in 1991, and save $9.7 million in the first year from changes to building industry safety accreditation.

Argued that the government's repeal day bills would deliver $2.1 billion in compliance savings and abolish bodies including the Fishing Industry Policy Council, and criticised Labor for introducing 21000 additional regulations while doing nothing to streamline schemes such as Comcare or the Do Not Call Register.

This bill would change how Australia handles people smuggling and asylum seekers both at sea and on land.
It would give the government stronger maritime enforcement powers, create temporary protection visas, and set up a fast-track assessment process for certain asylum claims.
The bill would let the minister cap the number of protection visas granted each year and remove the 90-day deadline for deciding such visas.
Reinforces maritime enforcement powers to stop people smuggling ventures at sea.
Introduces Temporary Protection Visas and Safe Haven Enterprise Visas for unauthorised arrivals who qualify for protection.
Creates a fast-track assessment process that bypasses the Refugee Review Tribunal for some applicants.
Codifies Australia's interpretation of its refugee obligations under the Refugees Convention into the Migration Act.
Retrospectively clarifies that children born to unauthorised maritime arrivals or transitory persons are also treated as such.
Restores the government's ability to set a statutory limit on protection visas granted per year and removes the 90-day decision requirement.

Asylum seekers who arrive illegally in Australia, including unauthorised maritime arrivals and transitory persons, as well as government officers and agencies involved in maritime operations and protection assessments.

Moved a bill to resolve Labor's legacy caseload of around 30,000 asylum claims, reintroducing temporary protection visas valid for up to three years and creating a new five-year Safe Haven Enterprise Visa for regional work, under which holders who work without income support for 3.5 years can apply for other onshore visas, and established a fast-track assessment process with a new Immigration Assessment Authority to replace merits review for unmeritorious claims.

Announced Labor will oppose the Migration and Maritime Powers Legislation Amendment bill in the House, objecting to a schedule that would render redundant a pending High Court case on turning back asylum boats, opposing the reintroduction of temporary protection visas, and citing government figures showing only 14 per cent of protection visa decisions now meet the 90-day rule, down from about half under Labor.
Argued that Labor is hypocritical in claiming the humanitarian high ground on asylum seeker policy, despite the outcomes of its own border protection record while in government.

Spoke in support of the bill, arguing that it would stop boat arrivals, address a 30,000-person legacy caseload, strengthen maritime enforcement, introduce temporary protection and safe haven enterprise visas, and support regional communities through work and study.

Moved a bill toughening job seeker compliance, noting 4.47 million of 12.75 million scheduled employment provider appointments were missed in 2013-14, a 35 per cent non-attendance rate, and that almost 280,000 job seekers, more than one in five, had a participation failure applied that year, while promoting the Restart program's incentive of up to $10,000 for employers hiring mature-age workers.

Argued that Labor supports mutual obligation and the bill's no-show, no-pay principle but opposes removing review rights, weakening protections for older job seekers, and extending delegation powers, while seeking assurances that suspensions will be notified promptly.

Supported stronger compliance for missed employment appointments, including suspension until attendance and removal of back pay for non-compliance, while arguing that reasonable excuses and safeguards for vulnerable job seekers would remain protected.

Questioned how job seekers delayed by severe weather, transport problems or other circumstances could give prior notice, and warned that suspending payments without adequate notice could further disadvantage people facing hardship.

Opposed the bill as punitive, arguing that it would penalise vulnerable job seekers, remove review rights and outsource compliance decisions to employment providers, while calling for job creation and describing barriers faced by job seekers in Bendigo.

Supported the bill as a measure to reinforce mutual obligation, arguing that people who miss appointments without satisfactory reasons should be required to comply, while saying that those facing serious disadvantage were not the intended target.

Supported the Job Seeker Compliance Framework bill, citing that almost 4.5 million of 12 million compulsory appointments in 2013-14 were missed, a 35 per cent non-attendance rate, cited British economist Stephen Nickell's research linking strict benefit enforcement to lower unemployment, and said from 1 January 2015 job seekers without a reasonable excuse would lose back-payment for missed appointments.

Supported the Job Seeker Compliance Framework bill, citing that 4.47 million of 12,750,000 compulsory appointments went unattended in 2013-14, a 35 per cent non-attendance rate, and that almost 280,000 job seekers, more than one in five, had a participation failure applied that year, and said from 1 January 2015 suspended payments would only be reinstated once a missed appointment was rescheduled and attended.

Supported the Job Seeker Compliance Framework bill's two-stage rollout, from 1 January 2015 requiring an attended appointment before reinstating suspended payments and from 1 July 2015 withholding back pay for unexcused absences, citing an attendance rate of only 65 per cent at compulsory appointments last financial year, and highlighted Trade Support Loans of up to $20,000 for apprentices.

Presented the Parliamentary Joint Committee on Human Rights' examination of the Counter-Terrorism Legislation Amendment (Foreign Fighters) Bill 2014, concluding that its declared area offence, carrying up to 10 years imprisonment, is likely incompatible with human rights because it reverses the presumption of innocence, and raised concerns about a new advocating terrorism offence that could criminalise speech through a recklessness test.

Introduced the Australian National Preventive Health Agency (Abolition) Bill 2014, arguing ANPHA duplicated Department of Health functions and was funded solely by the Commonwealth, and that abolishing it would remove overlap and reintegrate its alcohol, tobacco and obesity work into the department without cutting funding commitments.

Detailed the case against abolishing the Australian National Preventive Health Agency, established in 2010 after task force consultations with almost 1,000 stakeholders, saying Labor invested nearly $1 billion in a national partnership agreement on prevention that the coalition has since cut by more than $360 million, and said downloads of the My QuitBuddy smoking-cessation app rose from 19,000 to 55,000 in a single month during the Summernats event that draws over 100,000 people.

Supported abolishing the Australian National Preventive Health Agency, criticising it for spending $463,000 on a fat tax study despite evidence from Denmark that such taxes fail, and for spending about $263,000 on a fake music festival Facebook campaign that received only 244 likes, roughly $1,000 per like of taxpayer money.

Opposed abolishing the Australian National Preventive Health Agency, citing data showing 672,000 hospital admissions in 2011-12 could have been avoided with better primary care, noting a smoking-cessation app saw downloads triple to 55,000 after an ANPHA-funded promotion at Summernats, and warned her Lalor electorate's Mercy Health service, built for 90,000 people, will soon serve 200,000.

Argued the Australian National Preventive Health Agency duplicates the work of the federal Department of Health and six state health departments, noting no state government had ever engaged the agency since the bill's announcement, calling it a waste of taxpayer money.

Reflected on health economics, noting Australia's $130 billion health system spends about 45 per cent of that on just two per cent of the population near the end of life, and argued the country's 35,000 general practitioners, trained for at least a decade, are the true front line for effective preventative health, not standalone agencies like ANPHA.

Opposed abolishing the Australian National Preventive Health Agency, cited a Lancet study showing one in three Australians, or 5.2 million people, are now obese, an 80 per cent rise in 33 years, and criticized the assistant health minister for scrapping a healthy-eating website built over two years on the advice of a staffer who was formerly an alcohol lobbyist.

Defended abolishing the Australian National Preventive Health Agency as duplicative, since no state or territory government ever contributed funding to it, and credited existing Commonwealth efforts like the Measure Up campaign, running since 2006, for tobacco use falling by more than 40 per cent among both men and women over the past 33 years.

Supported abolishing the Australian National Preventive Health Agency, calling it a taxpayer-funded lobby group that both advocates for and receives government funding, citing an Institute of Public Affairs report finding a third of submissions to the original Preventative Health Taskforce came from bodies receiving large taxpayer funding.

Opposed abolishing ANPHA, citing $360 million in cuts to preventive health national partnership funding, and warned the Good Start Program supporting Maori and Pasifika health in the electorate of Rankin, home to almost 14,000 New Zealand-born residents, would lose funding from 1 July.

Opposed abolishing ANPHA, quoting the health minister's own second reading speech saying taxpayers should 'pick up the bill' for people who disregard health consequences, and highlighted men's health data showing men are four times more likely than women to die by suicide, an average of five a day.

Opposed abolishing ANPHA, citing a study finding preventive programs on smoking, road safety and heart disease prevented about 400,000 premature deaths between 1975 and 1995, saving $8.4 billion, far more than the agency's own $6.4 million budget.

Opposed abolishing ANPHA, criticising the minister responsible for preventive health, Senator Fiona Nash, for removing the healthy food-rating website and employing a former fast-food industry lobbyist as chief of staff, and cited AMA figures that 90 per cent of Australians have tried alcohol and 83 per cent drank in the past 12 months.

Summed up the ANPHA abolition bill, saying the agency represented symbolism over substance, spending taxpayer money on things like sponsoring burnouts at Summernats, and that its preventive health functions would continue more efficiently within the Department of Health.
